title: Retries Are Rent
summary:
Your retry loop does not bill you in tokens. It bills you in seconds you cannot buy back, and free capacity is the one lane where the second invoice is the only one that arrives. That is the whole argument. Everything below is a way to put a number on it before you hand a week of batch work to a queue you do not control.

Tokens are the visible line on the receipt. Wall clock is the line the vendor never prints. When you move a workload onto a free lane, the first line shrinks and the second one grows, and most teams never notice the trade because only one of the two numbers shows up in a dashboard.

The ledger you are not keeping

Every agent framework I read now ships a retry policy, and almost none of them log what a retry costs in time. So write the ledger yourself. The harness below is a proposal, not something I ran against a hosted endpoint, so treat the output as a placeholder until you point it at your own client.

# retry_ledger.py — proposal; run it against your own client before trusting it
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from time import monotonic

RETRYABLE = {"rate_limited", "timeout", "upstream_5xx"}

@dataclass
class Attempt:
    queue_wait_s: float
    work_s: float
    tokens_in: int
    tokens_out: int
    outcome: str

@dataclass
class Task:
    name: str
    attempts: list = field(default_factory=list)

    @property
    def succeeded(self):
        return bool(self.attempts) and self.attempts[-1].outcome == "ok"

    @property
    def wall_s(self):
        return sum(a.queue_wait_s + a.work_s for a in self.attempts)

    @property
    def queue_share(self):
        return sum(a.queue_wait_s for a in self.attempts) / max(self.wall_s, 1e-9)

    @property
    def tokens(self):
        return sum(a.tokens_in + a.tokens_out for a in self.attempts)


def run_task(name, call, max_attempts=4, backoff=1.5):
    task = Task(name)
    delay = 1.0
    for _ in range(max_attempts):
        t0 = monotonic()
        result = call(name)          # your client returns outcome + timing + usage
        t1 = monotonic()
        task.attempts.append(Attempt(
            queue_wait_s=getattr(result, "queue_wait_s", 0.0),
            work_s=t1 - t0 - getattr(result, "queue_wait_s", 0.0),
            tokens_in=getattr(result, "tokens_in", 0),
            tokens_out=getattr(result, "tokens_out", 0),
            outcome=result.outcome,  # "ok" | "rate_limited" | "timeout" | "malformed" | "bad_input"
        ))
        if result.outcome == "ok":
            return task
        if result.outcome not in RETRYABLE:
            return task              # do not buy rent on a bug you can fix
        delay *= backoff
    return task

Two lines in that dataclass matter more than the rest. queue_share tells you how much of your latency was someone else's scheduling, and tokens counts every attempt, not just the successful one. Log both and the free-lane decision stops being a vibe.

Failure classes decide who pays

Retrying a bad_input error is the most expensive habit in this whole space. You pay queue wait, you pay tokens, and the answer cannot change. Treat malformed the same way until you have a repair step that actually alters the request.

Retries are rent because the landlord is the queue, not your code. A three-attempt success at 12 seconds of queue wait each costs you 36 seconds of clock whether or not a single token was billed. On an interactive path that is a product failure. On an overnight batch it is a rounding error.

Where the free lane actually wins

Free capacity is a scheduling choice, not a discount. It wins when your deadline is loose, your tasks are idempotent, and your failures are retryable. It loses when a human is watching the spinner, or when retry amplification pushes you past a wall-clock deadline that has money attached.

Workload shape Free lane Committed lane
Interactive edit, p99 under 2s no yes
Overnight batch, morning deadline yes, if queue_share stays under ~50% yes if it does not
Fan-out where 30%+ attempts are rate_limited yes, with a jittered cap yes
Anything with bad_input in the loop fix the input first fix the input first
Long cross-repo refactor you must restart often risky: restarts multiply queue wait yes

That table is a starting point, not a benchmark. Fill in your own columns from the ledger after a few hundred tasks.

Where MonkeyCode fits in the ledger

The project currently advertises free model access and a free server option, which makes it a reasonable candidate for the slow lane in the harness above: batch jobs where you care about the total and not the tail. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

I am not going to quote a quota number here. Allowances, model availability, and server terms are set by the project and they move; read the current terms instead of a blog post, including this one. What matters for the ledger is only that you can point call() at it, capture queue wait if the client exposes timing, and count attempt-level tokens.

One natural way to start: take a batch you already run, cap max_attempts at two, run it twice — once on the lane you pay for, once on the free lane — and compare tokens / successes and wall_s / successes side by side. Two numbers, one afternoon.

Run 200 tasks and assert the ledger reports an amplification near 1.43 and a queue_share above 0.6. Then flip the stub to 2 seconds of queue wait and rerun. Do not use the free lane for anything with a human on the other end, for regulated data whose residency rules you have not confirmed, or for workloads you must restart often. And do not use any of this if you cannot state your per-success budget. A ledger without a target is a diary. Pick the number first, then let the queue wait tell you which lane you can afford.

title: Case Study: A Nightly Maintenance Worker That Rebuilds Its Own State After Every Restart
summary:
A nightly maintenance worker needs very little: a process that starts on schedule, one file of durable state, and a cheap way to label what it finds. What it really needs is to stay boring under failure, so you can ignore it for a month and still trust its output.

This case study covers one small project end to end — a worker that scans a handful of repositories for dependency drift, labels each finding, and writes a short digest. The scanning is easy. The hard part is the state handoff that lets the worker restart at any moment, on a host you do not administer, without double-posting or losing its cursor.

The trend feed this week is full of AI feature tours and open AI fatigue, and both reactions are reasonable. The useful counter-move is duller: wrap the probabilistic part in a deterministic shell, so a bad model day cannot corrupt your data.

Goal and non-goals

The goal fits in one sentence: given a list of repositories and pinned versions, produce one digest per day, at most once, with a resumable cursor and an auditable reason for every label.

The non-goals matter just as much, because they are what keeps the design small:

  1. No web dashboard, no database, and no queue broker.
  2. No multi-worker parallelism in version one.
  3. No upstream writes — the worker only reads tags and appends to its own state file.
  4. No strict dependence on any single model endpoint for correctness.

That last point is the design hinge. Classification quality is allowed to vary; the digest itself must not.

Decide where the worker lives before you write any code

Most teams skip this table and regret it later. Score your own options against your own constraints.

Option Survives laptop sleep Secret exposure Restart cost Reasonable fit
Your laptop cron No Low High, manual Prototyping only
CI scheduled job Yes Medium, in CI secrets Low Repos already in CI
Free server instance Usually Medium, in env vars Low if stateless One small worker, tolerant of restarts
Paid VM with a supervisor Yes Medium Low Delivery SLAs, regulated data

If your job touches regulated data, or another team depends on its output at a fixed hour, skip the free tier row entirely. The rest of this article assumes you accepted restarts as normal and designed for them.

The state file is the only durable contract

Write every piece of resumable knowledge into one JSON document, and treat that document as the interface between runs. Anything not in the file is reconstructed on startup.

{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "last_completed_run": "2026-10-15T02:10:04Z",
  "cursor": {"repo": "acme/etl", "last_tag": "v3.14.0"},
  "lease": {
    "owner": "worker-7f3c",
    "acquired_at": "2026-10-15T02:09:41Z",
    "heartbeat_at": "2026-10-15T02:09:52Z"
  },
  "recent_labels": [{"repo": "acme/etl", "tag": "v3.14.0", "label": "routine"}]
}

Two rules keep this file trustworthy. First, bump schema_version whenever the shape changes, and refuse to run on an unknown version. Second, only ever commit the file with an atomic rename, so a kill signal cannot leave a half-written document on disk.

import json
import os
import tempfile


def save_state(path, state):
    directory = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(path)) or "."
    fd, tmp = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=directory, prefix=".state-", suffix=".tmp")
    try:
        with os.fdopen(fd, "w") as handle:
            json.dump(state, handle, sort_keys=True)
            handle.flush()
            os.fsync(handle.fileno())
        os.replace(tmp, path)  # commit point
    except BaseException:
        os.unlink(tmp)
        raise

The os.replace call is the commit point, and everything before it is invisible to readers. If the process dies during the write, you lose a temporary file and nothing else. If it dies after the rename, the new state is simply the current state.

A lease that fails loudly instead of double-running

Two workers racing on the same cursor is the classic way a nightly job becomes a nightly outage. A lease with a heartbeat solves this without any coordination service, as long as you accept a bounded risk of a stale takeover.

from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

LEASE_TTL = timedelta(minutes=15)


def parse_ts(value):
    return datetime.fromisoformat(value.replace("Z", "+00:00"))


def lease_blocks_run(state, now, owner):
    lease = state.get("lease")
    if not lease:
        return False, "no lease recorded"
    age = now - parse_ts(lease["heartbeat_at"])
    if lease["owner"] == owner:
        return False, "we already own the lease"
    if age > LEASE_TTL:
        return False, "stale lease from %s" % lease["owner"]
    return True, "held by %s for %s" % (lease["owner"], age)

Heartbeat every few minutes, always with the current UTC timestamp, and log the reason string on every exit path. When someone asks why a run stopped, that line is the whole answer.

Model calls behind a deterministic fallback

The labeling step is where a model is genuinely useful and where a free tier is genuinely risky. Keep the call behind a function that can always return a value, and let a rules-based classifier own the default path.

ALLOWED = {"routine", "risky", "unknown"}


def classify(title, call_model, rules_fallback):
    try:
        label = call_model(title, timeout=20)
        if label in ALLOWED:
            return label, "model"
    except Exception as exc:
        print("model tier unavailable: %s" % exc)
    return rules_fallback(title), "rules"

Record the source (model or rules) next to every label. That single field turns a vague quality complaint into a queryable ratio, and it makes provider changes measurable instead of anecdotal.

The code above is a proposal you can run locally with a stub call_model, not a published benchmark. Nothing in this design depends on a specific endpoint, model name, or provider — which is exactly why it survives a free tier changing underneath you.

Where the free tier fits this design

The worker needs two things outside your laptop: a host for the process and an endpoint for the labeling step. MonkeyCode provides free model access and a free server option, which matches both needs in the shape this design already expects. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

Treat free availability as operator-supplied and time-sensitive. Token allowances, rate limits, data retention, and instance lifetimes on free tiers change, so read the current terms on the official site before you schedule anything that matters, and keep the rules-based fallback in place so a policy change degrades quality instead of halting the job.

Results: what each failure does to the run

The value of this structure is not speed; it is a short, predictable list of failure behaviors. Verify each row yourself with the harness below.

Failure Expected behavior
Killed mid-write Temporary file discarded, previous state intact
Two workers start together Second worker exits with the lease reason logged
First worker hangs Lease goes stale after the TTL, next run takes over
Model endpoint unavailable Labels fall back to rules and are marked as such
State file schema changed Preflight exits non-zero instead of guessing

Notice what is absent: no partial digest, no duplicated post, no silent data loss. Every failure mode is either a clean refusal or a degraded-but-labeled result.

Two commands to run before you trust it

Write a preflight check and run it as the first step of every scheduled execution. It should parse the state file, compare schema_version, verify the lease, and check clock skew against a known time source.

python -m worker.preflight --state .state/worker.json && \
  python -m worker.run --once

Then test idempotency directly, because this is the property that actually breaks in production. Run the worker twice in a row against an unchanged input set, and diff the state file after each pass.

python -m worker.run --once && cp .state/worker.json /tmp/after-first.json
python -m worker.run --once && diff /tmp/after-first.json .state/worker.json

A clean run should update last_completed_run and nothing else. If the cursor moves on the second pass, your idempotency assumption is wrong, and no amount of logging will save you.

Limitations and who should not use this

This approach trades throughput and guarantees for simplicity, and that trade is not always right.

  • Do not use it if your job must run at an exact minute with an SLA, because free hosts restart, throttle, and cold-start without warning.
  • Do not use it for regulated or customer-identifying data, because you do not control retention on a free endpoint.
  • Do not use it for multi-writer workflows, because a single lease file assumes one logical writer at a time.
  • Do not use it if you need sub-minute latency or persistent local disk, since both assumptions are gone on ephemeral hosts.
  • Do not skip the fallback classifier, because a free model tier is a shared resource with shared availability patterns.

If your job sits in any of those categories, the table at the top of this article points you elsewhere, and that is a legitimate outcome.

What I would change next

The next iteration is to make the digest itself a contract: fix the key order, the label vocabulary, and the timestamp format, then assert them in preflight the same way you assert schema_version. After that, add one integration test that starts two processes against a shared state directory and asserts that exactly one of them reaches the labeling step. Those two checks catch the overwhelming majority of failures you will actually see in the first year.

If you want to try the loop without provisioning anything, start by running the preflight check on a free server instance and letting it complete a single pass before you add a schedule.

What follows is a copy-paste workflow built on evidence TTLs. Every gate artifact carries an issue time and an expiry. Anything missing, unreadable, or stale blocks promotion by default.

Why a clean pass is only a snapshot

Model progress is currently outrunning release process. That gap shows up in the boring places, not in benchmarks.

  • Model defaults drift. A provider re-points an alias, and your "verified" output shape changes.
  • Free-tier policy drifts. Rate limits, allowed regions, and idle shutdown rules are not contracts.

  1. PASS — fresh evidence exists, it says PASS, and it is inside its TTL.
  2. ESCALATE — evidence exists but is expired or partially complete. A human must re-run the gate and re-issue the record.
  3. BLOCK — evidence is missing, unreadable, negative, or future-dated. Promotion stops with no override path in the script.

Assign a TTL to every artifact

Two files. One declares the gates and their TTLs; the other reads the evidence records and returns an exit code your CI can branch on.

Gate declarations 

# gates.yaml

gates:

    evidence: .evidence/model_pin.json

The 60-line checker

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Fail-closed gate checker.

Exit codes:
  0 = all gates PASS
  2 = at least one gate ESCALATE (stale, human re-run required)
  1 = at least one gate BLOCK (missing, unreadable, negative)
"""
import datetime as dt
import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import yaml  # pip install pyyaml

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
ORDER = {"BLOCK": 0, "ESCALATE": 1, "PASS": 2}


def now_utc():
    return dt.datetime.now(dt.timezone.utc)


def parse_ts(value):
    return dt.datetime.fromisoformat(value.replace("Z", "+00:00"))


def evaluate(name, spec, clock):
    path = ROOT / spec["evidence"]
    if not path.exists():
        return "BLOCK", f"{name}: no evidence file at {spec['evidence']}"
    try:
        record = json.loads(path.read_text())
    except (json.JSONDecodeError, OSError) as exc:
        return "BLOCK", f"{name}: unreadable evidence ({exc})"
    if record.get("result") != "PASS":
        return "BLOCK", f"{name}: last result was {record.get('result')!r}"
    if not record.get("command"):
        return "BLOCK", f"{name}: record has no reproducible command"
    try:
        age_h = (clock - parse_ts(record["issued_at"])).total_seconds() / 3600
    except (KeyError, ValueError) as exc:
        return "BLOCK", f"{name}: bad issued_at ({exc})"
    if age_h < 0:
        return "BLOCK", f"{name}: evidence is dated in the future"
    ttl = float(spec["ttl_hours"])
    if age_h > ttl:
        return "ESCALATE", f"{name}: {age_h:.1f}h old, ttl {ttl:.0f}h"
    return "PASS", f"{name}: fresh ({age_h:.1f}h / {ttl:.0f}h), owner {spec.get('owner')}"


def main():
    config = yaml.safe_load((ROOT / "gates.yaml").read_text())
    clock = now_utc()
    verdicts = [evaluate(n, s, clock) for n, s in config["gates"].items()]
    for verdict, message in sorted(verdicts, key=lambda v: ORDER[v[0]]):
        print(f"[{verdict:8}] {message}")
    if any(v == "BLOCK" for v, _ in verdicts):
        return 1
    if any(v == "ESCALATE" for v, _ in verdicts):
        return 2
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

  1) echo "do not promote" ; exit 1 ;;

TTLs fail in practice for one reason: re-running the gates costs money or attention, so teams stretch the TTL until the gate is meaningless.

The lever that makes the loop survivable is cheap execution. This is where MonkeyCode is relevant to the workflow: the project is open source, and it publishes a free model allowance plus a free server option.   • The free model allowance covers the prompt-contract and output-shape checks whose results expire fastest.
  • Your own repo stays the source of truth. If the evidence cannot be regenerated from a committed command, the gate is not trustworthy no matter where it ran.

  1. Does every gate in gates.yaml have an owner and a TTL?
  2. Does every evidence file exist, parse, and carry result: PASS?
  3. Does every record include the exact command that produced it?
  4. Is every record inside its TTL, and none future-dated?
  5. Can a second person reproduce one random record from scratch?
  6. Is the quota headroom check less than 24 hours old?
  7. Did the rollback drill actually restore the previous version, with a log digest attached?
  8. Is the egress review still accurate for the credentials the build currently holds?

title: An incident report nobody could open, an extension that wanted my token, and 80 lines instead
summary:
The report nobody could open

We write incident reports as single HTML files: inline CSS, an inline SVG timeline, no build step, one file you can read in ten years. They live in a private GitHub repository next to the code they are about.

Nobody could open them. GitHub shows an .html file as source, and the "download it, then double-click it" workflow is where reading stops for most people. GitHub Pages would render them, but Pages on a private repository is an Enterprise feature. GitHub's PDF viewer exists, but these are not PDFs.

The extension that wanted my token

There is a Chrome extension for exactly this problem. I read its code before installing it. It asks for a GitHub token (a personal access token, or an OAuth grant with full repo scope), sends that token to the author's server, and the server fetches your file and renders it on the author's domain.

That is a lot of trust for a preview button. An incident report is the most sensitive document a team writes, and the fix was to hand the key to the whole repository to a stranger's Lambda.

The other option, a userscript, keeps the token in the browser but resolves the short-lived tokenised link GitHub issues for a private file and passes it, as a URL parameter, to the author's website, which loads the file from there. The link to your private file lands in that site's address bar, history and hosting logs.

Both are honest projects, and the idea of a button beside Raw is theirs. I just did not want the file to leave the browser.

The Raw button already does the hard part

Click Raw on a private file and watch the network tab. GitHub answers github.com///raw// with your own session, then redirects to raw.githubusercontent.com with a token that expires in minutes. That host serves the file as text/plain, which is why it is never rendered, and sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *. And github.com's Content Security Policy allows connections to it.

So a script running on the file page can do what Raw does, and then fix the only thing that was wrong, the content type:

const tab = window.open('', '_blank');                    // open inside the click, so popup blockers allow it
const response = await fetch(location.pathname.replace('/blob/', '/raw/'), { credentials: 'same-origin' });
const html = await response.text();
tab.location.href = URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([html], { type: 'text/html' }));

That is the whole mechanism. The only network request is the one GitHub itself makes for Raw. No server, no token, no account, no site other than github.com in the path. The rendered page lives at a blob: URL in your browser, with no cookies and no access to GitHub.

80 lines instead

The result is unraw: a userscript that adds an unraw button next to Raw on every .html file page, and a bookmarklet for people who do not want to install anything. The button copies Raw's classes and data-* attributes so it matches GitHub's current styling, and a MutationObserver puts it back after GitHub's client-side navigation. The rest is the snippet above with error handling. Your userscript manager shows you all of it before installing; it is about 80 lines.

Two limits, both inherent to the approach. Pages that reference relative files (./style.css, img/x.png) render without them, because those paths do not exist at a blob: URL; self-contained pages render completely, and inlining is the right habit for documents you want to read from GitHub anyway. Inline scripts run inside the blob: page, isolated from GitHub, so treat a preview the way you would treat opening a downloaded copy.

The rule that produced the tool is the rule that keeps it small: the file may not leave your browser. Anything that would need a server or a token will not be added.

  • Install page, with the bookmarklet: https://thangaram611.github.io/unraw/
  • Userscript on Greasy Fork: https://greasyfork.org/scripts/600316-unraw
  • Source, MIT, with a comparison table drawn from each tool's code: https://github.com/thangaram611/unraw

title: Decide Where the Agent Runs With a Four-Axis Fit Ledger
summary:
Every week brings another round of confident model announcements, and every week my review queue looks roughly the same as it did a month earlier. That gap is not a scandal and it is not a mystery to me; it is a routing problem that most teams never name out loud. We keep asking which model is best when the operationally useful question is which compute tier this specific unit of work should run on. I have been answering that question with a four-axis ledger instead of a price tag, and what follows is the entire workflow with runnable code.

Three tiers show up in that ledger: a free hosted tier, a paid hosted tier, and self-hosted compute. A concrete example of the first is MonkeyCode's free model access, which the operator describes as including free model access plus a free server option, with a free allowance reported at ten million tokens. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. I have not audited those numbers, so treat them as claims to verify inside your own account rather than constants to plan around.

Conclusion First: Price Is the Last Question, Not the First

When a free tier appears, the instinct is to route everything to it and celebrate the savings on Monday. That instinct fails for a boring reason: the expensive part of agent work was never the token bill, it was the human time spent catching bad output. A free generation that costs me forty minutes of review is more expensive than a paid generation I can trust on the first pass.

So I stopped optimizing for price and started optimizing for fit. Fit means the tier matches the data boundary, the reversibility of the output, the patience of the waiting human, and the blast of a missed error. Price is a derived quantity that falls out of those four answers, not an input you start from.

So why do so many teams still open the pricing page first? Because price is the only number that arrives pre-formatted on a marketing site. The other three axes require you to measure your own work, which is slower and far more honest.

The Four Axes That Actually Decide the Route

  1. Egress class. Can the prompt and its context leave your boundary, or does it contain internal and regulated material? This axis has veto power over every other consideration.
  2. Output reversibility. If the result is wrong, can you delete it with no cleanup, or does it land in a branch, a ticket, or a production path? Throwaway output tolerates a weaker tier.
  3. Latency budget. How long will a human actually wait before they switch windows and lose the thread? This is a measurement, not a feeling.
  4. Cost of a wrong answer. What happens if the error ships and nobody catches it before Friday? High cost buys review, not a fancier model.

Notice that nothing on that list mentions price per million tokens. That is deliberate, because price only becomes meaningful after the four axes have already narrowed the field.

Step 1: Write the Policy Before You Write the Router

I keep the policy in a file so the arguments happen in review rather than inside my head at midnight. The thresholds below are placeholders, and you should replace each one with your own measured numbers.

# policy.yaml
axes:
  egress_class: [public, internal, regulated]
  reversible: [true, false]
  latency_budget_s: [interactive_10, batch_600]
  wrong_answer_cost: [low, medium, high]

routes:
  - when: {egress_class: regulated}
    tier: self_hosted
    note: 'boundary rule, no hosted call at any price'
  - when: {egress_class: internal}
    tier: self_hosted
  - when: {egress_class: public, reversible: true, wrong_answer_cost: low}
    tier: free_hosted
    note: 'output gets discarded, nothing downstream depends on it'
  - when: {egress_class: public, latency_budget_s: interactive_10}
    tier: paid_hosted
    note: 'measure your own p95 before you trust this line'
  - default: true
    tier: paid_hosted

Step 2: Implement the Router as a Pure Function

The router should be boring, deterministic, and easy to test, which means no network calls and no hidden state. Here it is as a single file with no dependencies beyond the standard library.

# route.py
from dataclasses import dataclass
from enum import Enum
from typing import Literal

class Tier(str, Enum):
    FREE_HOSTED = 'free_hosted'
    PAID_HOSTED = 'paid_hosted'
    SELF_HOSTED = 'self_hosted'

Egress = Literal['public', 'internal', 'regulated']
Cost = Literal['low', 'medium', 'high']

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Task:
    name: str
    egress_class: Egress
    reversible: bool
    latency_budget_s: int
    wrong_answer_cost: Cost

def route(task: Task) -> tuple[Tier, str]:
    if task.egress_class in ('regulated', 'internal'):
        return Tier.SELF_HOSTED, 'rule 1: the data boundary beats every other axis'
    if task.reversible and task.wrong_answer_cost == 'low':
        return Tier.FREE_HOSTED, 'rule 2: throwaway output over public data'
    if task.latency_budget_s <= 10:
        return Tier.PAID_HOSTED, 'rule 3: interactive budget, check your own p95'
    return Tier.PAID_HOSTED, 'rule 4: default until you have evidence to move'

Two things deserve emphasis here. First, the first matching rule wins, and I ordered them so that the unglamorous boundary rule can never be overridden by a clever saving. Second, every return carries a reason string, because a router that cannot explain itself is impossible to debug when it misroutes.

Step 3: Split Authoring From Verification

Here is the part that changed my workflow the most: authoring and verification do not need the same tier. Authoring is probabilistic and touches your context, while verification is deterministic and touches your repository.

That split means I can run generation on whichever tier the axes allow and send the test suite somewhere cheaper, as long as the repository itself is clean. Verification on a disposable workspace is exactly the kind of job a free server option fits, because the output is a pass or fail rather than a mergeable artifact.

def route_verification(task: Task, repo_has_secrets: bool) -> tuple[Tier, str]:
    if task.egress_class != 'public':
        return Tier.SELF_HOSTED, 'verification still crosses the same boundary'
    if repo_has_secrets:
        return Tier.SELF_HOSTED, 'build logs can echo environment state'
    return Tier.FREE_HOSTED, 'deterministic job, disposable workspace, no secrets'

That guard clause is not paranoia; build logs leak more credentials than anyone expects. Run a coarse preflight before you hand a repository to any hosted runner.

# coarse preflight, not a replacement for a real secret scanner
git grep -nIE '(AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}|-----BEGIN [A-Z ]*PRIVATE KEY-----)' -- . \
  && echo 'key-like material in tracked files: stop and self-host' \
  || echo 'no obvious key material found in tracked files'

Step 4: Prove the Router With Labeled Tasks

A policy file that only lives in your head drifts within two weeks, so I pin expectations in a test. These cases represent my labeled decisions, not universal truths, and the suite protects consistency rather than correctness.

# test_route.py
import pytest
from route import Task, Tier, route, route_verification

CASES = [
    (Task('summarize internal incident', 'internal', True, 5, 'low'), Tier.SELF_HOSTED),
    (Task('rename vars in sample repo', 'public', True, 5, 'low'), Tier.FREE_HOSTED),
    (Task('rewrite prod migration', 'public', False, 900, 'high'), Tier.PAID_HOSTED),
    (Task('generate throwaway fixtures', 'public', True, 600, 'low'), Tier.FREE_HOSTED),
]

@pytest.mark.parametrize('task,expected', CASES)
def test_route(task, expected):
    tier, reason = route(task)
    assert tier is expected, reason

def test_verification_refuses_dirty_repo():
    task = Task('run unit tests', 'public', True, 600, 'low')
    assert route_verification(task, repo_has_secrets=True)[0] is Tier.SELF_HOSTED

Run it with pytest -q. When a case fails after a policy edit, you get to argue with your past self instead of guessing, which is the entire point of writing the policy down in the first place.

Step 5: Change Rules, Not Cases

Every misroute gets one line in a log, because patterns only appear after you stop explaining incidents away. The log is plain JSON Lines so the Friday review ritual stays cheap and boring.

printf '%s\n' '{"task":"fixture rewrite","chosen":"free_hosted","problem":"output was merged, not discarded","fix":"make reversible an explicit input"}' >> misfits.jsonl
jq -r '.fix' misfits.jsonl | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head

The rule I follow is simple: if the same fix shows up twice in a month, I amend the policy instead of adding a third exception. Exceptions rot quietly, while a changed rule is visible to everyone who reads the file. My review hour is short because most of the questions were already answered on Monday.

Where Free Access and a Free Server Fit

The free tier earns its place in route two: public data, throwaway output, low wrong-answer cost. Fixture generation, sample-data munging, docstring drafts, and "explain this stack trace" all land there comfortably, because a bad answer costs me nothing but a rerun.

The free server option fits the verification half rather than the authoring half, which surprised me at first. Deterministic test runs, lint passes, and build checks produce no mergeable artifact, so there is nothing to review and nothing to regret. Keep credentials out of the workspace and the boundary question mostly answers itself.

What I do not do is pretend the free tier is an availability guarantee. Operator-supplied allowances, quotas, and server terms change, and any workflow that breaks when they change was never a workflow; it was a bet.

The Decision Table I Use

Situation Route Reasoning
Regulated or internal data Self-hosted The boundary rule outranks every price argument
Public data, throwaway output, low error cost Free hosted Nothing downstream depends on the result
Public data, output gets merged, medium or high error cost Paid hosted plus human review You are buying accountability, not tokens
Interactive loop under ten seconds Paid hosted Replace this row with your own measured p95
Deterministic verification, no secrets in the repo Free server Disposable workspace, repeatable result
Credentials in tracked files Self-hosted Build logs can echo environment state

Limitations and Who Should Skip This

The thresholds in my policy are placeholders calibrated against my own task mix, so yours will differ and probably by a wide margin. The router also cannot see your repository, which means the secret preflight stays a separate step that a human has to remember.

Free-tier availability, quotas, and free server terms are operator-supplied claims here rather than promises, so I keep a manual override for the days when a tier misbehaves. Self-hosting is not free either; it trades a bill for maintenance time, patching, and someone who gets paged at an inconvenient hour.

Who should skip this? If you run one task type against one repository, the ledger is ceremony, and a single documented default will serve you better. If your team has no review process, routing will not save you, because the fourth axis is unknowable until someone is accountable for misses. And if a compliance review of hosted egress has not finished, stay self-hosted and revisit the table later.

What I Would Do Next

Start by labeling ten real tasks from last week against the four axes, then route them by hand before you write any code. You will probably find that two rules cover most of your work and that the free tier is bigger than you expected. If you want a hosted free tier to pressure-test that third route against your own task list, that is a cheap first stop before committing budget anywhere else.

Step 5: Change Rules, Not Cases

Every misroute gets one line in a log, because patterns only appear after you stop explaining incidents away. The log is plain JSON Lines so the Friday review ritual stays cheap and boring.

Where Free Access and a Free Server Fit

The free tier earns its place in route two: public data, throwaway output, low wrong-answer cost. Fixture generation, sample-data munging, docstring drafts, and "explain this stack trace" all land there comfortably, because a bad answer costs me nothing but a rerun.

The free server option fits the verification half rather than the authoring half, which surprised me at first. Keep credentials out of the workspace and the boundary question mostly answers itself.

What I do not do is pretend the free tier is an availability guarantee. Operator-supplied allowances, quotas, and server terms change, and any workflow that breaks when they change was never a workflow; it was a bet.

The Decision Table I Use

Situation Route Reasoning
Regulated or internal data Self-hosted The boundary rule outranks every price argument
Public data, throwaway output, low error cost Free hosted Nothing downstream depends on the result
Public data, output gets merged, medium or high error cost Paid hosted plus human review You are buying accountability, not tokens
Interactive loop under ten seconds Paid hosted Replace this row with your own measured p95
Deterministic verification, no secrets in the repo Free server Disposable workspace, repeatable result

Limitations and Who Should Skip This

The thresholds in my policy are placeholders calibrated against my own task mix, so yours will differ and probably by a wide margin. The router also cannot see your repository, which means the secret preflight stays a separate step that a human has to remember.

Free-tier availability, quotas, and free server terms are operator-supplied claims here rather than promises, so I keep a manual override for the days when a tier misbehaves. If your team has no review process, routing will not save you, because the fourth axis is unknowable until someone is accountable for misses. Start by labeling ten real tasks from last week against the four axes, then route them by hand before you write any code. You will probably find that two rules cover most of your work and that the free tier is bigger than you expected. title: I Audited Ten Million Free Tokens. The Ledger Drifted First.
summary:
I Audited Ten Million Free Tokens. The Ledger Drifted First.

My free allowance didn't evaporate because a model was slow. It evaporated — inside the simulation I built to check it — because my retry wrapper paid for the same prompt twice while my streaming parser paid for the answer zero times. Two bugs, opposite signs, almost cancelling.

That's the dangerous case, isn't it? A near-cancel looks like "fine." And "fine" is how a token budget turns into a Monday incident instead of a Friday cleanup.

Everyone is wiring agents onto free model access right now; that's the mood of the timeline this week. So the interesting question isn't whether a free model is good enough. It's whether your ledger agrees with theirs, and what it means when it stops agreeing.

Three probes, one table

I built one harness and ran it three ways. Probe A reconciles my own token sum against the total the platform reports, and logs the sign of the drift. Probe B tags every attempt so I can count the duplicate prompt tokens my own retry policy manufactures. Probe C asks what a repair costs when a stream ends without a usage block at all.

Three probes, one SQLite table, standard library only. No SDK, no framework, no dashboard.

I pointed the endpoint variables at MonkeyCode's free model access, since that's the free tier I had a key for. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

The harness 

# ledger.py -- stdlib only. Probes A/B/C behind one table.
import hashlib, json, os, sqlite3, time, urllib.request

BUDGET = int(os.environ.get("TOKEN_BUDGET", "10000000"))  # operator-supplied allowance
DB = os.environ.get("LEDGER_DB", "ledger.sqlite")

def conn():
    c = sqlite3.connect(DB)
    c.execute("""CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS calls(
        id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, ts REAL, attempt INTEGER, phash TEXT,
        ptok INTEGER, ctok INTEGER, estimated INTEGER, status INTEGER, ms INTEGER)""")
    return c

def phash(payload):                      # dedupe key for retry accounting
    return hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()[:16]

def approx(text):                        # char/4, always flagged, never invoiced
    return max(1, len(text) // 4)

def post(payload):
    url = os.environ["MC_BASE_URL"].rstrip("/") + "/chat/completions"
    req = urllib.request.Request(
        url,
        data=json.dumps(payload).encode(),
        headers={"Authorization": "Bearer " + os.environ["MC_API_KEY"],
                 "Content-Type": "application/json"},
    )
    t0 = time.time()
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=120) as r:
        body = json.loads(r.read())
        return body, r.status, int((time.time() - t0) * 1000)

def send(payload, attempt=1):
    body, status, ms = post(payload)
    u = body.get("usage") or {}
    est = 0 if u else 1
    ptok = u.get("prompt_tokens") or approx(json.dumps(payload))
    content = body.get("choices", [{}])[0].get("message", {}).get("content", "") or ""
    ctok = u.get("completion_tokens") or approx(content)
    c = conn()
    c.execute("INSERT INTO calls(ts,attempt,phash,ptok,ctok,estimated,status,ms) "
              "VALUES(?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?)",
              (time.time(), attempt, phash(payload), ptok, ctok, est, status, ms))
    c.commit()
    return body, est

def reconcile(server_total, used):
    c = conn()
    mine = c.execute("SELECT SUM(ptok+ctok) FROM calls").fetchone()[0] or 0
    dup  = c.execute("SELECT SUM(ptok) FROM calls WHERE attempt > 1").fetchone()[0] or 0
    est  = c.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM calls WHERE estimated=1").fetchone()[0]
    drift = mine - server_total
    if abs(drift) > 0.02 * max(used, 1):
        verdict = "unexplained drift -- halt and re-run the fixture"
    elif est:
        verdict = "estimated rows present -- totals are not invoice-grade"
    elif used > 0.7 * BUDGET or used + drift > 0.7 * BUDGET:
        verdict = "close to the line -- reconcile before the next run"
    else:
        verdict = "accounting closed"
    return {"harness": mine, "server": server_total, "drift": drift,
            "retry_duplicate": dup, "estimated_rows": est,
            "pct_of_budget": round(100 * drift / BUDGET, 4), "verdict": verdict}

# arithmetic check -- injects known defects, never touches the network
python ledger.py --fixture 240 --drop-usage 0.03 --retry-rate 0.04

# the live probe, pointed at whatever your own console exposes
TOKEN_BUDGET=10000000 MC_BASE_URL="$BASE" MC_API_KEY="$KEY" python ledger.py --probe all

Note what I deliberately did not do: hardcode a model name. Read the identifier off your own console and put it in the payload, because a blog post is the worst possible source of truth for a string that changes without telling you.

The run, and what I'm willing to publish

Here's where I have to be precise, because the whole value of this account depends on not laundering numbers. The table below comes from the fixture. It is not a measurement of any shared endpoint, and I'd be lying by framing if I presented it as one.

The fixture injects two known defects: dropped usage blocks on 3% of responses, and a retry policy that re-sends full prompts. If the harness arithmetic is right, the two injected causes must sum to the drift exactly. That's the test.

field value how it is produced
harness total 9,730,412 SUM(ptok+ctok) across 240 rows plus retries
server counter 9,625,304 the fixture's simulated counter
drift +105,108 harness minus server
retry duplicate 63,900 SUM(ptok) WHERE attempt > 1
dropped-usage rows 7 rows with estimated=1
dropped-usage tokens 41,208 known value the injector removed
drift check 63,900 + 41,208 = 105,108 ✅ exact, by construction
share of budget 1.05% drift / 10M

So what did I learn about the free tier? Nothing — and that's the point. I learned the harness closes. If you cannot make your own accounting agree with itself on a fixture where you already know the right answer, you will never correctly interpret a 1% drift against a live counter. You'll just argue about it.

And notice the shape of the failure. One defect under-counted, one over-counted, and the budget looked almost honest. Free tiers don't usually fail loudly. They fail symmetrically.

Where this actually breaks

Retry amplification is the first killer, and it's yours, not theirs. A dropped connection doesn't refund the prompt you already sent. If your wrapper resends the full conversation, you pay twice for identical input, and the second payment buys you nothing but a retry.

Stream truncation is the second, and it fails the other way. When a stream dies before the usage block arrives, a naive wrapper records zero completion tokens for an answer you definitely received. Now your ledger is optimistic, which is worse than pessimistic, because optimism is invisible until the invoice disagrees.

Tool-call loops are the third. An agent that re-reads the same file six times to answer one question isn't broken — it's just expensive, and no per-request counter will tell you which loop did it. You need the phash column for that, and you need to actually look at it.

Concurrency races are the fourth, and they're the one a single-machine harness cannot fix. If something else is using the same key while your cron job runs, your drift will change sign between runs and you'll spend a week blaming the provider. Add a run identifier and compare runs, not instants.

A decision table I'll defend

signal what it probably means action
drift under 0.5%, zero estimated rows your wrapper agrees with the counter keep the 70% soft alarm and stop optimizing
drift 0.5–2%, retry_duplicate ≈ drift retries, not the platform cap attempts at 2, dedupe by phash, re-run fixture then probe
estimated_rows > 0 a stream ended before usage arrived treat totals as unknown until that probe runs non-streaming
drift flips sign between runs you're measuring concurrency you don't control scope the key to the harness, or stop trusting the series
drift above 2% of budget cause genuinely unknown treat the allowance as unbounded risk and move the workload

That last row is the important one. "Free" is a price, not a guarantee about accounting. If you cannot reconcile it, you cannot plan on it.

The free server, kept small

My harness needs to run every six hours, write one SQLite file, and keep a key off my laptop. That's a cron job with a file attached — not a platform migration. A free server option is enough for exactly that, and that's the only reason it belongs in this article.

The reason it matters is failure isolation, not compute. If the host disappears tomorrow, my ledger is a file I can move, and the fixture still passes on my machine. If your experiment can't survive losing its host, you built a dependency, not a measurement.

The operator also describes the project as open source. If that matters to you, go read the client before you trust anything above — including its own counter. Verify first, then benchmark.

Who should not do this

Don't use this approach if your reconciliation has to tie to invoiced currency. A free-tier counter is a signal, not an invoice, and no amount of harness engineering changes that.

Don't run the harness on a hosted free server if your payloads carry data with residency or classification constraints. The experiment isn't worth the incident.

Don't bother if the workload is a one-off script you'll delete on Friday. Two hundred lines of ledger code is overkill for a throwaway.

And don't adopt a retry-heavy streaming repair loop on a metered free allowance if you can't tolerate paying twice for the same prompt. Sometimes the honest answer is fewer retries, not a better ledger.

The takeaway

Your free tokens are a budget, not a vibe. Measure the drift, name its cause, and decide before the allowance does it for you.

If you want the harness and somewhere to run it, MonkeyCode is where I pointed mine — bring the fixture first, and trust the arithmetic before you trust anybody's dashboard.

title: GUML: Let the Model Write 24 Lines and the Compiler Write the Other 229
summary:
TL;DR: GUML is a tiny, indentation-based UI language designed to be written by a language model, and a Rust compiler that turns it into React, Svelte 5, static HTML, Web Components, a JSON UI tree, A2UI or MCP-UI. The model writes 24 lines. The compiler writes the fetch, the abort, the retry with backoff, the stale-while-revalidate cache, the optimistic update, the rollback and the accessible names: 253 lines of React for the task app below. Every error comes back in one pass, with a code and a suggestion, and the obvious ones are fixed without asking the model again.

cargo install guml-cli     # the `guml` command
pnpm add @guml/core        # the same compiler as WebAssembly
pip install guml           # and from Python

🔗 GitHub · 📦 @guml/core on npm · 📄 Research report

Table of Contents

  1. Why I built this
  2. The 24-line argument
  3. A tour of the language
  4. Inside the compiler
  5. A lexer that cannot decide alone
  6. Every error in one pass
  7. Did you mean card?
  8. Repair without a model
  9. What 24 lines become
  10. Seven backends, one vocabulary
  11. Themes and capabilities
  12. What is measured, and what is not
  13. A real model tried it
  14. The playground and the chat
  15. Proof: what I ran for this post
  16. What I found while writing this
  17. The question still open
  18. What I learned
  19. What's next
  20. Try it

Why I built this

Ask any AI app builder for a task list and watch what comes back: two hundred lines of React. useState, useEffect, an AbortController, a loading flag, an error flag, an optimistic update, a rollback, a className string per element, and aria-labels if you're lucky.

Almost none of that is a decision. It's convention: the same fetch-with-cancellation shape, the same rollback, the same focus ring. The model is being paid, in tokens, in latency and in error probability, to re-derive a compiler's output by hand, every single time.

Tailwind makes the point sharply. className="mt-6 flex items-center justify-center gap-3" is about fourteen tokens that express three tokens of intent: row, centered, normal gap.

So the question behind GUML is simple: what if the model only wrote the decisions, and a compiler wrote the conventions? There's no widely used representation that sits between "natural-language prompt" and "framework source code". Every AI builder jumps the whole distance in one hop. GUML is the stop in the middle.

Diagram from the original.

The dashed box is the whole idea. Nothing in it appears in the source the model writes, so the model can't spend tokens on it, and it can't get it wrong.

The 24-line argument

This is the task-list fixture, fixtures/b.guml, complete:

page Tasks

type Task {id, title, done:bool, createdAt:date}
data tasks:Task[] GET /api/tasks
  add  POST   /api/tasks      {title} optimistic:prepend
  save PATCH  /api/tasks/{id} {done}  optimistic
  drop DELETE /api/tasks/{id}         optimistic

state draft=""
state filter=all|open|done

head Tasks — {tasks.open.count} open

form >tasks.add{title:draft}; draft=""
  input draft aria="New task" placeholder="Add a task…"
  btn Add primary disabled={!draft.trim()} busy="Adding…"

tabs filter

list tasks where={filter}
  check {done} >tasks.save
  text {title} strike={done}
  btn Delete quiet aria="Delete {title}" >tasks.drop
  empty Nothing here yet.

Read it once and you know the whole app: a typed resource with three mutations (two of them optimistic), a text draft, a three-way filter, a live count in the heading, a form, tabs, and a list with an empty state.

Here it is compiled in the browser. This is the docs playground running the Rust compiler as WebAssembly:

Notice the small line under the input: tabs — not lowered by this compiler version. The in-browser preview renderer doesn't draw tabs yet, and it says so instead of drawing something approximate. That's one of the project's four invariants, and it'll come up again.

A tour of the language

The whole syntax fits in a paragraph, which is the point: the full spec plus the vocabulary costs a model about 2,935 estimated tokens of prompt, and the spec file states a budget of 3,000.

Lines are structure. Indentation is nesting, 2 spaces per level. No closing tags, no braces for blocks, no imports. A tab is an error (GUML0001).

Directives declare the data model:

page Counter title="Clicks"                 // name -> component
type Task {id, title, done:bool}           // fields default to string
state count=0                              // type inferred from the initial value
state filter=all|open|done                 // an enumerated domain; first value is initial
data tasks:Task[] GET /api/tasks           // a resource
  add  POST   /api/tasks      {title}  optimistic:prepend
on {filter} >tasks.list                    // an effect: re-runs when filter changes

Elements are tag [positionals] [name=value] [>action]. Positionals can be a label, a modifier, a {binding}, a /route or an #anchor. The action comes last because > swallows the rest of the line.

Bindings are read-only expressions: paths, comparison, boolean logic, arithmetic, and a fixed set of aggregates (.count .sum .open .done .trim .lower .upper). {tasks.open.count} is "how many rows have the bool field unset". It works on invoices too, where the bool is paid, because the compiler reads the flag from the row type rather than from a name it hoped for.

Actions are statements separated by ;: >count++, >count=0, >tasks.add{title:draft}; draft="".

The vocabulary is closed. There are 49 primitives in a registry (card row col section nav hero form tabs list table btn input select metric modal toast…), 24 modifiers (primary ghost quiet danger sm lg center between…), and 12 global attributes. There is no class attribute: presentation belongs to the theme.

def declares a user component. It's a compile-time macro with parameters and one slot, and by the time codegen runs there's no trace of it.

Two conformance levels. core is markup only: no I/O, no state, meant to be safe to render from an untrusted agent. app adds state, data, actions and the repeaters. An app construct at the core level is GUML0091.

Escape hatches. js and raw blocks pass through verbatim and unchecked. Each one emits a GUML0090 note, so the escape-hatch rate stays countable. That rate is one of the things the research measures.

Inside the compiler

The compiler is a Rust workspace of 14 crates, about 33,000 lines. The heaviest are guml-compiler (about 10.7k lines, the analysis passes) and guml-codegen (about 9.1k lines, the backends).

The driver is short enough to quote. From crates/guml-compiler/src/lib.rs:

// ...
expand::expand(&mut program, &mut diagnostics);      // def macros
sema::analyse(&program, reg, &mut diagnostics);      // scope + accessibility
validate::validate(&program, reg, &mut diagnostics); // structure, methods, unused
types::check(&program, &mut diagnostics);            // expression types, aggregates

All the analysis passes always run, even after an error, so diagnostics accumulate. Codegen runs only on an error-free program. There's no separate IR: the AST, guml_ast::Program, is what every backend consumes, and each backend lowers expressions through one shared function.

The type checker is the newest stage and, according to the docs, the one that paid for itself most directly. It found a live bug in a published example where {invoices.open.count} had been compiling to a filter on a field the type didn't declare: always zero, and no test noticed.

A lexer that cannot decide alone

GUML has an ambiguity no lexer can resolve on its own. The comment at the top of crates/guml-syntax/src/lib.rs puts it in two lines:

btn Decrement ghost >count--      // Decrement is a label, ghost is a modifier
p Press the buttons to change.    // the whole remainder is prose content

Same shape, opposite meanings. Whether the rest of a line is structure or prose depends on the tag, and the tag's kind lives in the registry. So the lexer produces both readings of every line: a token list and the raw text. Then the parser, which knows the registry, picks one.

The rule is subtle: a text tag stays prose unless the line contains an = whose name the registry accepts for that tag. So p Set x=1 to enable is prose, and text {title} strike={done} is structure. Step through it:

A frame from the interactive sketch in the original — watch it run.

Two more lexer decisions I like:

  • Actions terminate the line by construction. Everything after > is one token, so actions are lexable in a single pass with no lookahead.
  • URLs are an allow-list. A route is /path at token start, so $24/mo stays one word, and absolute URLs are limited to http:// and https://. As the comment says, a general "scheme followed by ://" rule would make javascript: and data: lexable as request targets. The allow-list is the security boundary.

Every error in one pass

This is the invariant I'd defend hardest, and the project's own CLAUDE.md says it plainly: "Each repair-loop round is a full LLM generation; single-error reporting is a product defect, not a style preference."

A compiler that stops at the first error is fine for a human, who fixes one thing and presses save. For a model it's a disaster: each round trip is a full generation, billed at output rates. So the parser recovers from everything:

  • An unknown tag is reported, with a suggestion, and then parsed as a container anyway, so errors in its children still surface.
  • A missing attribute value is reported and parsing continues.
  • Bad indentation is reported once per run, not once per line. Before that fix, one mis-indented section produced 15 stray GUML0011s, and a repair loop handed sixteen errors will edit sixteen lines, fifteen of which were correct.

Diagnostic codes are an API

There are 49 codes, GUML0001 to GUML0104, grouped in decades: lexical, layout, syntax, resolution, semantics, accessibility, types, structure, domains, escape hatches. They're append-only: a test enforces it, and the Rust enum is #[non_exhaustive]. The reason is that a repair loop keys on them, so GUML0033 has to mean the same thing forever. 0060 is deliberately unallocated, because "shipping a code with no emit site is how a diagnostic surface starts lying about what it can detect."

Every diagnostic is machine-actionable JSON:

{"code":"unknown_tag","id":"GUML0030","severity":"error","message":"unknown tag `crad`",
 "span":{"start":27,"end":31,"line":4,"col":1},"help":"did you mean `card`?","suggestion":"card"}

suggestion is present only when the fix is unambiguous, which is what lets a machine apply it without asking anyone.

Did you mean card?

How does the compiler know crad means card? The obvious answer is edit distance, and the obvious answer is wrong. Plain Levenshtein scores crad → card as 2 (two substitutions), which is too far for a four-letter word. Typos are very often swapped neighbours, so GUML uses Optimal String Alignment, which adds one more case to the recurrence:

$$
d(i,j)=\min\begin{cases}
d(i-1,j)+1 & \text{delete}\
d(i,j-1)+1 & \text{insert}\
d(i-1,j-1)+[a_i \neq b_j] & \text{substitute}\
d(i-2,j-2)+1 & \text{if } a_i=b_{j-1} \text{ and } a_{i-1}=b_j
\end{cases}
$$

Watch the two tables fill, and see where the transposition (highlighted) saves an edit:

The threshold is at most 1 edit for names of four characters or fewer, and at most 2 above that. But edit distance can't help with the most common mistake a model makes, which is writing HTML out of habit: button → btn is three edits. So before any distance is computed, the registry checks a table of 39 HTML habits (div→col, span→text, button→btn, hr→divider, ul→menu, dialog→modal…), and each entry carries a note explaining why GUML doesn't have that element.

Modifiers are stricter still: exactly one edit, on a word of at least four characters. That rule exists because of a real data-loss bug, where btn Click me was "fixed" to btn Click md.

Repair without a model

Models don't return clean files. They return Here you go:, a code fence, the code, another fence, and Let me know if you want changes!. guml repair strips that packaging and applies every unambiguous fix, with no model call, ever:

What 24 lines become

Here's the part the model never writes. These excerpts are real output from guml build fixtures/b.guml, 253 lines of React and TypeScript in total.

A retry helper that knows what's safe to retry. It uses exponential backoff (300 ms, then 600 ms), only for idempotent methods, only on a network failure or a 5xx, and never after an abort:

async function retrying(url: string, init: RequestInit = {}, tries = 3): Promise<Response> {
  const idempotent = !init.method || ["GET", "HEAD", "PUT", "DELETE"].includes(init.method);
  let wait = 300;
  for (let attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
    const last = attempt >= tries || !idempotent;
    try {
      const res = await fetch(url, init);
      if (res.ok || res.status < 500 || last) return res;
    } catch (err) {
      if (last || (err instanceof Error && err.name === "AbortError")) throw err;
    }
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, wait));
    wait *= 2;
  }
}

A cache with stale-while-revalidate and in-flight deduplication. It caches GETs only, treats entries as stale after 30 seconds (a constant, deliberately "not a knob"), serves the last good data if a refresh fails, and lets mutations invalidate by URL prefix, so PATCH /api/tasks/{id} invalidates /api/tasks:

async function cached<T>(url: string, init: RequestInit = {}): Promise<T> {
  const method = init.method ?? "GET";
  const key = `${method} ${url}`;
  if (method !== "GET") return read<T>(url, init);
  const hit = GUML_CACHE.get(key);
  const fresh = hit && Date.now() - hit.at < GUML_STALE_MS;
  if (hit && !fresh) {
    void refresh<T>(key, url, init).catch(() => {});
  }
  if (hit) return hit.data as T;
  const pending = GUML_INFLIGHT.get(key);
  if (pending) return pending as Promise<T>;
  return refresh<T>(key, url, init);
}

A list fetch that can be cancelled, with an alive guard so a late response never writes into an unmounted component:

const tasksList = useCallback(() => {
  const controller = new AbortController();
  let alive = true;
  setTasksLoading(true);
  setTasksError(null);
  cached<Task[]>("/api/tasks", { signal: controller.signal })
    .then((rows) => { if (alive) setTasks(rows); })
    .catch((err: unknown) => {
      if (!alive || (err instanceof Error && err.name === "AbortError")) return;
      setTasksError(err instanceof Error ? err.message : "Unknown error");
    })
    .finally(() => { if (alive) setTasksLoading(false); });
  return () => { alive = false; controller.abort(); };
}, []);

And the optimistic update with rollback, all from the word optimistic:prepend:

const tasksAdd = useCallback(
  async (body: Partial<Task>) => {
    const snapshot = tasks;
    setTasksSaving(true);
    const optimistic = { id: `tmp-${Date.now()}`, ...body } as Task;
    setTasks((prev) => [optimistic, ...prev]);
    try {
      const res = await retrying("/api/tasks", {
        method: "POST",
        headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
        body: JSON.stringify(body),
      });
      if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Request failed: ${res.status}`);
      invalidate("/api/tasks");
      const created = (await res.json()) as Task;
      setTasks((prev) => prev.map((it) => (it === optimistic ? created : it)));
    } catch (err: unknown) {
      setTasks(snapshot);
      setTasksError(err instanceof Error ? err.message : "Could not save");
    } finally {
      setTasksSaving(false);
    }
  },
  [tasks],
);

The design goal is that backends share decisions rather than copy them: one element table (element_for(tag)), one design-system table (theme::active().classes(tag, mods)), one expression lowering (expr::lower_in) and one liveness answer (referenced_names, which deliberately over-approximates so codegen never drops a declaration the output still mentions).

The element table exists because of a bug. The HTML backend once had a fallback of _ => "div", so the no-JavaScript build had no landmarks. Now a test checks that every tag lowers to the same element in every backend.

The A2UI emitter is labelled honestly: it was "written from a description of the protocol rather than against its published JSON schema". Actions become declared intents, so no JavaScript travels in the payload.

Themes and capabilities

A theme is data, with a contract

There are no class strings in GUML source, so all presentation comes from a theme. A theme is JSON: rules mapping (tag, modifiers) to classes, plus a contract the compiler enforces. From crates/guml-codegen/src/theme.rs:

pub fn validate(&self) -> Result<(), ThemeError> {
    if self.contract.focus_visible.trim().is_empty() {
        return Err(ThemeError::WeakContract(format!(
            "theme `{}` declares no `contract.focus_visible`; a control nobody can see focus on \
             is unusable from a keyboard, and the compiler cannot supply one it does not know", self.name)));
    }
    if self.contract.min_contrast < 4.5 {
        return Err(ThemeError::WeakContract(format!(
            "theme `{}` declares `min_contrast` {}, below the WCAG AA floor of 4.5 for body text", ...)));
    }
    Ok(())
}

The compiler appends the contract's focus and disabled classes to every focusable element itself, "so a theme cannot forget it on one control". That's what lets a themeable compiler still promise accessible output. Two themes are built in: stock tailwind (the default) and shadcn, which uses shadcn/ui's own oklch tokens, so a host already running shadcn drops it in unchanged.

Compression isn't uniform, and the reason is prose. In the landing page, 232 of GUML's 376 tokens are the human copy itself, which costs the same in any language. Structure is only 144 tokens in GUML, against about 1,416 in React. So the ratio follows a simple curve:

There's one exploratory run with a real model, and it's reported because a negative result is worth reporting. Six small apps were generated by Llama 3.1 8B Instruct on build.nvidia.com, with the shipping prompt (about 3,073 estimated tokens), temperature 0.2, one generation each:
